Making Helm Autonomous

A grounded read of three research inputs against what Helm already does — and a prioritised, honestly-costed set of upgrades that move the app from recommender toward a self-improving, self-governing portfolio manager. Effort is prototype-scale (Helm's React/HTML + optional in-app Claude calls), not a production trading desk.
Architect's analysis · Jul 2026
The three inputs
Blueprint · portfolio-specific

The Self-Driving Portfolio

Ang, Azimbayev & Kim · Apr 2026

~50 specialist agents run the full SAA pipeline: macro regime → asset-class CMAs (via an LLM-as-judge over 7 methods) → 20+ competing portfolio-construction methods → peer review + Borda voting → a CIO ensemble + board memo. A meta-agent compares past forecasts to realised returns and rewrites agent code/prompts. The IPS governs everything; autonomy (L0–L5) is a policy dial.

Method · the learning loop

SAMULE — Multi-level Reflection

Ge et al., AWS AI Labs · Sep 2025

Self-learning from failures, not rare wins. Reflection is synthesised at three levels: micro (one failed trajectory → specific fix), meso (many trials of one task → error taxonomy), macro (errors clustered across tasks → transferable rules). Plus foresight reflection: predict the next outcome, and when reality diverges, trigger a reflection mid-stream.

Framework · lifelong learning

Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning

Cai et al., ECNU / Shanghai AI Lab · Dec 2025

Four principles for a self-evolving agent: Experience Exploration, Long-term Memory, Skill Learning (abstract recurring patterns into reusable skills, then Add / Update / Delete / Combine them), and Knowledge Internalisation. Three shifts: passive→proactive, context→memory, imitation→learning.

Where Helm sits on the autonomy ladder

The blueprint borrows the SAE self-driving levels (L0–L5). Helm today is roughly L2: it analyses, scores, and proposes fully-costed trades across accounts, but a human reads and executes every one (the new Trade-log makes that a one-click record, not an order). The upgrades below are what it takes to reach L3–L4 — the paper's own operating band — without ever pretending to place real orders.

L0
Manual
Human does all analysis & decisions.
L1
Assisted
Tool computes; human interprets everything.
Helm today
L2
Recommends
Engine proposes scored, routed trades; human approves & executes each.
Target
L3
Conditional
Acts within IPS bounds; escalates edge cases; human ratifies a book.
L4
Supervised-auto
Self-rebalances & self-improves within domain; human oversees the loop.
L5
Full
Autonomous across all regimes. Not a goal for a personal book.
The lever is the IPS, not the code. As in the paper, tightening the governing document (risk budget, floors, escalation triggers) pulls the same engine toward supervision; loosening it moves toward autonomy. Autonomy becomes a setting you dial, not a rebuild.
What Helm already implements (in primitive form)

Encouragingly, Helm is further up the blueprint than it looks — much of the scaffold exists. The upgrades are mostly about closing loops and letting existing modules act, not building from zero.

1 · Multi-method competition & deliberation Self-Driving Portfolio §3.4–3.6
Stop trusting one construction method. Run many, let them critique & vote, ensemble the survivors.
1
M
effort

PC method registry — grow 3 presets into a competing roster

Next
Add equal-weight, inverse-vol, min-variance, max-diversification, CVaR, tail-parity and the paper's max-entropy method alongside the existing HRP, each producing a full book from the same signals + covariance.
Helm today: helmConstruct already does HRP + Ledoit-Wolf and 3 risk presets — the covariance plumbing is there; this adds objectives to a registry.
Pros
  • Ensemble robustness — no single-method fragility (DeMiguel 2009)
  • Reuses existing covariance + signals
  • Sets up voting & ensembling (#2, #3)
Cons
  • More methods to maintain & explain
  • Marginal edge for a concentrated retail book
  • Compute grows with method count
2
L
effort

Strategy review — peer critique + Borda vote + diversity floor

Later
Each method reviews two peers (one same-family, one cross-family), then a modified Borda count (top-5 ranking + a bottom flag) blends with a quant score. A diversity constraint forces ≥3 of 4 method families into the shortlist — surfacing consensus and dissent.
Helm today: nothing equivalent — the 3 presets don't critique each other.
Pros
  • Auditable committee-style rationale (fiduciary-friendly)
  • Guards against a single school monopolising the book
  • Directly implements the paper's core mechanism
Cons
  • Needs LLM calls (cost + nondeterminism) or rule proxies
  • Heavy machinery for one user's book
  • Voting quality depends on genuinely diverse priors
3
M
effort

CIO ensemble judge + board memo

Next
Combine the surviving methods with a regime-conditional ensemble and emit a short board memo: the chosen allocation, why, the biggest positions, changes since last review, key risks, and what would invalidate it.
Helm today: methods.jsx already weights 8 lenses by regime — extend that to weight portfolios, and generate the memo prose.
Pros
  • One defensible book + a written, checkable rationale
  • Closes the human-oversight loop cleanly
  • Reuses the per-regime weighting you already have
Cons
  • LLM-written memo risks lookahead bias on history
  • "Automation surprise" if the memo is rubber-stamped
4
S
effort

Adversarial diversifier sleeve

Later
One deliberately-contrarian candidate that maximises orthogonality to the consensus book (subject to a Sharpe floor) — it surfaces allocations no consensus method would find, then earns a small ensemble weight.
Helm today: helmConstruct's diversification overlay is a seed; this is the explicit orthogonal-to-centroid version.
Pros
  • Cheap way to widen the opportunity set (boosting analogy)
  • Reduces pairwise overlap across candidates
Cons
  • Poor standalone metrics can confuse the UI
  • Only meaningful inside an ensemble (needs #1/#3 first)
2 · The self-improvement loop Self-Driving Portfolio §5.3 · SAMULE
The highest-leverage move: let Helm read its own track record and propose changes to itself — safely.
5
L
effort

Close the Learning-Lab loop: propose → approve → apply

Now
Today the validator only watches. Let it propose concrete config edits — factor weights, score thresholds, gate params — each backed by walk-forward evidence, gated by the §17 acceptance criteria, applied only on your one-click approval, fully logged and one-click revertible.
Helm today: learninglab.jsx has the walk-forward engine, candidate-rule library, and version registry — but it's sandboxed and never touches the live engine. This wires the approved-change path.
Pros
  • Genuine self-improvement, human-in-the-loop & reversible
  • Builds directly on the existing version registry
  • Turns the Lab from a demo into the engine's brain
Cons
  • Overfitting risk — needs strict acceptance gates + embargo
  • Long horizon before out-of-sample proof
  • Requires discipline to not chase every proposal
6
M–L
effort

Multi-level reflexion ledger (micro / meso / macro)

Now
SAMULE's structure, applied to trades: micro = post-mortem on each closed position (predicted vs realised, what the signal missed); meso = an error taxonomy per ticker/strategy; macro = transferable rules clustered across regimes & themes (e.g. "trend-gate fails in liquidity-drain regimes"). Failure-centric by design.
Helm today: this is the standing open todo (reflexion ledger). Tracker's realized-since already marks proposals to the live feed — the raw material exists.
Pros
  • Turns every loss into a structured, queryable lesson
  • It's the evidence feed that powers #5
  • Learns from failures — abundant, unlike wins
Cons
  • Cold-start: weak until outcomes accrue over months
  • Needs honest attribution (EV-error by regime/theme/horizon)
3 · Memory & skills Experience-Driven Lifelong Learning · harness techniques
Give the engine a memory it acts on, and let it bank what works as reusable skills.
7
M
effort

Structured experience memory (Add / Update / Delete / Combine)

Next
Beyond scattered localStorage journals: one persistent, queryable store of decisions, outcomes, and self-notes that the engine reads before acting, and actively curates with the ELL four operations so it never bloats.
Helm today: several localStorage journals exist (tracker, papersim, real-trades) — this consolidates them into an addressable memory with retrieval.
Pros
  • Continuity across sessions → personalisation over time
  • The substrate reflection (#6) writes into
  • "Context → memory" shift from the ELL framework
Cons
  • Retrieval + curation design work
  • Browser storage limits; may need export/sync later
8
M
effort

Skill library — capture a good run as a reusable skill

Later
When a decision pattern works repeatedly (e.g. "trim into strength when RSI>70 & quality high"), distil it into a named, validated skill the engine can reapply and reason about — the ELL "imitation → learning" shift.
Helm today: the candidate-rule library in the Lab is the closest thing; skills would be user-earned, not pre-authored.
Pros
  • Compounding, transparent competence
  • Skills are inspectable & removable (unlike weights)
Cons
  • Risk of banking luck as "skill" — needs a validation gate
  • Curation burden as the library grows
9
S–M
effort

Foresight reflection — predict, compare, flag surprise

Next
SAMULE's interactive trick: record an explicit expectation per open position (path + invalidation level); when reality diverges beyond a band, auto-trigger a reflection and surface an alert — proactive, not post-hoc.
Helm today: tracker's realized-since compares proposals to price after the fact; this makes the expectation explicit and the divergence an active trigger.
Pros
  • Early error detection instead of quarterly review
  • "Passive → proactive" with modest effort
Cons
  • False alarms if the expectation bands are miscalibrated
  • Needs the memory (#7) to store expectations well
4 · LLM-as-judge Self-Driving Portfolio §3.3 (CMA judge)
Layer qualitative judgment on top of the quant scorer — bounded, and with a written rationale.
10
M
effort

Judge layer for signal / CMA selection

Next
Wrap the rule-based scorer with a judge that reads the candidate estimates + regime + valuation + signals and selects or blends with explicit weights and a one-line rationale — hard-constrained to stay within the candidate range (the paper's key guardrail).
Helm today: window.claude.complete is already wired in analysis.jsx — the plumbing exists; this applies it at the selection step with a range constraint.
Pros
  • Qualitative judgment + audit trail, on top of quant
  • API already integrated — low plumbing cost
  • Range constraint keeps it honest
Cons
  • Lookahead bias — the model knows market history
  • Nondeterministic; cost per call; needs caching
  • Must never override the quant range bound
5 · Governance & the autonomy dial Self-Driving Portfolio §5.2
One governing document, one dial — the safe way to hand over more control.
11
S–M
effort

Formalise Plan into a real IPS the whole engine reads

Now
Promote the Plan page to a single governing document — investable universe, risk budget, per-sleeve floors/caps, and escalation triggers — that every module reads and checks compliance against (a CRO-style compliance line on each proposed book).
Helm today: plan.jsx holds required return, risk budget & horizon — a proto-IPS. This makes it the enforced boundary, not just a display.
Pros
  • One control surface for everything downstream
  • Prerequisite for safe autonomy (#5, #12)
  • Fiduciary-style, checkable audit trail
Cons
  • Upfront work to wire compliance checks everywhere
  • Only as good as the triggers you write
12
M
effort

Autonomy dial (L0–L5)

Later
A single setting for how much Helm may do on its own: recommend-only → auto-log with approval → auto-propose a rebalance within IPS bounds, escalating anything that breaches a trigger. Matches the paper's L3–L4 band.
Helm today: effectively fixed at "recommend-only"; the dial makes autonomy an explicit, reversible choice.
Pros
  • Earns trust gradually, on your terms
  • Same engine, different policy — no rebuild
Cons
  • Needs the guardrails (#5, #11) in place first
  • Execution stays manual — no broker API (by design)
6 · Optional — not sequenced flagged, not prioritized
Ideas worth knowing about, not committed to a phase. Add if/when they earn their place.
13
M
effort

Learn from your overrides — the signal the engine doesn't read yet

Optional
Every layer above — meta-agent, reflexion ledger, skill library — learns from the engine's own trade history. The sharpest point in the harness/context research: the one signal that can't be gamed is a human override. You already generate it constantly — accept/reject in Portfolio Simulation, edits in the Trade Log, Tracker's journal — but nothing reads it back in.
Helm today: confirmed — signalsFor() is called from papersim.jsx, tracker.jsx, screener.jsx and the CIO panel, but it's a one-way function; your decision logs are stored but never consulted. Wiring it up: log a pattern each time you override (e.g. "rejected 4 straight Buy signals on high-beta names in a Markdown crypto phase") → surface it as a procedural-memory note next time the pattern recurs → soften/harden confidence, never silently change the call.
Pros
  • Cheapest possible context-layer win — no new agents, no new infra, pure signal you already produce
  • The one memory source that reflects your judgment, not the engine's own biases
  • Low risk — only ever adds a caveat, never silently overrides output
Cons
  • Noisy on a small sample — needs enough overrides to see a real pattern vs. a fluke
  • Risk of a confirmation-bias loop (learning to please you, not to be right) without care
Risks the papers flag — and Helm's hard limits

Lookahead / data-contamination bias

Any LLM was trained on market history, so an LLM-judge (#3, #10) "knows" the past — clean historical backtests are impossible with it. Keep LLM judgment on live-forward decisions; keep backtests purely quantitative (as the Learning Lab already does).

LLM monoculture

If every agent shares one base model, their errors correlate. Mitigate by keeping deterministic quant methods in the mix (Helm's strength) and only using the model where genuine judgment adds value.

Automation surprise

The failure mode of aviation autopilots: operators stop paying attention. The board memo (#3) and approve-step (#5) exist precisely to force genuine engagement, not rubber-stamping.

Self-modifying-code safety

An engine that edits its own config (#5) needs guardrails: acceptance gates, a version registry, and one-click revert — all of which Helm's Lab already scaffolds. Never auto-apply without the approve step.

Hard limit — no execution

Helm has no brokerage connection and never will place orders. Every "autonomous" step ends at a proposal or a logged record; you still trade at NBDB. Autonomy here means analytical autonomy, honestly scoped.

Hard limit — no model retraining

Helm can't fine-tune or update model weights (SAMULE's retrospective model, SEAL-style self-adapting weights). It does the harness-level version — improving prompts, config, memory and skills — which is where the leverage is for a client-side app anyway.

Close the loop
highest leverage, lowest new-surface-area
  • #6 Reflexion ledger (micro/meso/macro)
  • #5 Learning-Lab propose→approve→apply
  • #11 Formalise the IPS
Phase 2 · judgment & memory
Add judgment
builds on Phase 1's evidence base
  • #10 LLM-as-judge (range-bounded)
  • #3 CIO ensemble + board memo
  • #7 Experience memory
  • #9 Foresight reflection
  • #1 PC method registry
Phase 3 · deliberation & control
Hand over control
only once the guardrails are proven
  • #2 Peer review + Borda voting
  • #4 Adversarial diversifier
  • #8 Skill library
  • #12 Autonomy dial (L0–L5)
Effort key: S ≈ a focused session · M ≈ a few sessions · L ≈ a sustained build with iteration. All estimates are prototype-scale within Helm's React/HTML architecture plus in-app Claude calls — not production-desk figures.
